- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially in early-to-mid horizon.
- When sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33), model underestimates; increase early forecast values, especially if price is trending down.
- Model often overshoots after sharp sentiment spikes (e.g., sentiment jumps to 1.00), leading to inflated mid-to-late horizon values; apply dampening factor to peaks.
- If history shows mean reversion (e.g., price oscillates around 2.00–2.10), model should not overreact to short-term sentiment shifts; anchor forecasts near historical mean unless sentiment strongly diverges.
- For 30-day forecasts, model frequently overestimates early days (day 1–5) when sentiment is neutral or slightly positive — reduce early forecast values if sentiment is weak or mixed.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “1.00” spikes followed by “0.00” drops, model tends to overcorrect — anticipate and slightly underforecast the next spike to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is high but price history is flat, model may overreact — apply a “sentiment-to-price” scaling factor <1.0 to prevent runaway growth.
- If sentiment is low and price is trending down, model often fails to recognize the trend — increase forecast decay rate or apply a downward bias to later horizon values.
